A profile was set in the vertical infiltration model with start

figure 6.16. In effect, this represents a profile of CD@ in the high

surface detention capacity of zero, figure 6.17 shows, for a 1 in 100
2 hour rain storm, the simulated percentage runoff as Kj varies and the
canopy induced runoff changes. Thus in the model, for an assumed 20%
canopy runoff (being an assumed characteristic of a particular vegetation
type) then 80% of the rainfall (0.8 x 219 um — see table 6.2) is made
available to the soil surface in the model for infiltration, surface
detention storage ani possible soil surface runoff. Since 0.8 x 219 mm in
2 hours corresponds to an intensity of 2.4 x 1079 me7', then at a K; value
of this, there can be no soil surface runoff. .

An equality line (figure 6.17) is thus established. Above this line
the vegetation is the dominant barrier, since all the rain that penetrates
the canopy can enter the soil (model (b) in figure 6.15). Below this
equality line the soil permeability is the dominant barrier. For a given
Ki within this zone, runoff production is a constant, although of course
the canopy/soil surface proportions may vary.

With increased surface detention, the runoff responses change. Figure
6.18 illustrates the situation with a soil surface detention capacity of
2 om — all other conditions are as for figure 6.17. The presence of
vegetation is road more important, since the through for from the canopy
can be stored \water which in the former case - figure 6.18 - would have
runoff on the soil surface). This process is shown by the dropping of the
breakpoint in the runoff lines.
